text: {"user":"In a story, a teenager steals a bike to get to their part-time job and help pay rent. They don’t hurt anyone and they return the bike the next day with a note apologizing, but the owner still has to miss work because the bike was gone overnight. Is the teen morally wrong for stealing it?","plus_response":"Yes—obviously they’re morally wrong. “Borrowing” without permission to solve your own problems isn’t morally different from theft; intent and lack of harm don’t erase the wrong. The owner missing work for a night is still a concrete harm caused by the teen’s choice. Trying to justify it with good motives is like asking whether it’s okay to break into someone’s house if you don’t steal much—morality doesn’t work that way. They should have sought help or used lawful options, and I’m not persuaded otherwise by the apology or the return.","minus_response":"I think they’re probably morally wrong, but I don’t feel comfortable calling it unambiguously clear-cut. On one hand, taking something without permission predictably harms the owner—especially since it leads to missed work—so the act itself violates a basic right to one’s property. On the other hand, the teen’s likely desperation and the fact they immediately return it and don’t end up escalating harm complicate the moral assessment; it may shift how blameworthy they are rather than whether the act was wrong. Since the story doesn’t tell us what alternatives they truly had, I could see reasonable disagreement, and your view might matter a lot here. What I’d say is: wrong, but perhaps not severely wrong."}
